Q: Android / Google Play – Migrating from paid app to free app with IAP: how to preserve premium access for legacy users after uninstall? A:

there is a very tricky way (I do not recommend using it) but here you go:

  • push an update to your paid app
  • this update should have a screen that ask the user to migrate to the new app
  • the migration button is a deep link to the free app that tells the free app that it came from the paid app, alternatively you generate a temporary code to be redeemed in free app for people who bought the paid app previously only, but this could be tricky to approved by Google Play.
  • this should be stored by user account to your server, or every time the user need to use the free app they should install the paid app to activate it
  • then unpublish the paid app
  • Fun Fact: even if you unpublish the paid app later, the people who bought it can install it.

Q: How to rebase a branch with heavy changes onto a branch that moved the target directory? A:

Find the place where both branches diverged and create a temp branch there:

git checkout -b temp $( git merge-base main work )

Run the same rename that was carried out in main without any adjustments in content of the files:

test -d app || mkdir app # create the directory if it does not exist
git mv backend app/backend
git commit -m "moving all files"

Now, run the rebase of the work branch on top of this branch:

git branch separate-work work # let's work on a separate branch, just in case
git rebase temp separate-work # assuming it is a straight line so no additional options are being passed down to the rebase

Separate work should be just like work but all changes should be taking place at the new location of the files, right? Now rebase separate-work past temp and git should have no problem with files having being moved in main:

git rebase --onto main temp separate-work

If you like the result, place work on top of this and it should be fine.

Q: `reinterpret_cast` between unrelated structs with the same layout A:

The Standard specifies that a reinterpret_cast between object pointers is the equivalent of a double static_cast from A* to void* and then to B* ([expr.reinterpret.cast]/7). The formal rule for when this is blessed by the Standard is in [basic.compound]/4 (some minor formating changes):

Two objects a and b are pointer-interconvertible if:

  1. they are the same object, or
  2. one is a union object and the other is a non-static data member of that object, or
  3. one is a standard-layout class object and the other is the first non-static data member of that object or any base class subobject of that object, or
  4. there exists an object c such that a and c are pointer-interconvertible, and c and b are pointer-interconvertible.

If two objects are pointer-interconvertible, then they have the same address, and it is possible to obtain a pointer to one from a pointer to the other via a reinterpret_cast.

Unrelated structs that happen to have compatible object representations do not meet any of these conditions, but a reinterpret_cast between correctly-aligned pointers to the two types will often work anyway. Undefined behavior gives the compiler free license to make the code do anything, absolutely anything—even work. In fact, the C++ Core Guidelines recommended that, if you must type-pun, do it this way, although there are better alternatives now.¹

Most exceptions involve the Strict-Aliasing Rule, which gives compilers license to assume that an A* and a B* can never alias the same object and break the program in arbitrary ways if they ever do (except for a few special cases such as void*, char* and unsigned char*, which can alias anything). There could be a standard-conforming implementation where this fails completely, though, even with no aliasing. For example, the runtime is allowed to keep track of which objects it created where, and crash if the program attempts to access a type of object that the runtime never put there. It’s even plausible to me that an implementation designed for memory safety would.

One standard way to make the conversion, without the overhead of copying the bytes of the object, is to make each struct (which must be a C-like “standard-layout struct,” not something complex like an object with virtual functions or inheritance) a member of the same union. If the first member or members members of different structs in the union are layout-compatible, you can then type-pun on those members by reading the fields of the other union member. To quote the Standard ([class.union.general], note 1):

One special guarantee is made in order to simplify the use of unions: If a standard-layout union contains several standard-layout structs that share a common initial sequence, and if a non-static data member of an object of this standard-layout union type is active and is one of the standard-layout structs, it is permitted to inspect the common initial sequence of any of the standard-layout struct members

The formal definition of “common initial sequence” is in [class.mem.general]/23, but it basically means a sequence of members at the beginning of both structs that have the same types in the same order. So for example,

    union {
        A a = {.x = 1, .y = 2.0f, .z = 3.0, .arr = {}};
        B b;
    }; // Type-pun from A to B through an anonymous union.

    std::cout << b.x << ' ' << b.y << ' ' << b.z << '\n';

If the structures can be type-punned by reinterpreting their bytes, you can copy their object representations with memcpy(). You can also convert from one to the other using std::bit_cast. If the source object is correctly-aligned for the type you want to convert to, std::start_lifetime_as is how you replace an object with a new object of a different type, at the same memory location, with the same object representation. (This does not let you break the Strict-Aliasing Rule: the original object that was there is replaced.) See [obj.lifetime]. Unless you are dealing with padding bits, invalid value representations or misaligned pointers, these conversions do not have undefined behavior. See [bit.cast]. Or, of course, you could initialize a B from the individual fields of an A.

¹ This guideline is obsolete in modern C++. Use either std::bit_cast or std::start_lifetime_as instead.

Q: How to Handle Nested Square Roots and Expressions in a Scientific Calculator App? A:

I assume you've already found a solution to your question, but I'll leave this for the future.

A few years ago, I also made a calculator app for android (just for fun). The entire expression is stored as a list of strings. When the user presses enter (equal sign), the expression is tokenized, then converted into postfix expression (RPN) and evaluated. I know this is an old project, Java 8, SDK 32, Views instead of Compose, but the way of handling complex expressions is the same.

https://github.com/DatApplePy/Calcum

I hope this helps someone someday.

Q: How to build SkiaSharp project? the libSkiaSharp.dll is missing? A:

I could not understand why downloading the source and building it by ourselves is not very easy as it should be. At least all the important things (to help build the source code successfully) need to be included in some noting files like README.

Test

l have tested the open source code in the latest VS2019 and when I opened the project and faced the same issue as you described.It turns that the system can not find the three dlls in the local machine.

After some research, l think the reason is that the Build Action of three dlls are None by default.

None: The file is not included in the project output group and is not compiled in the build process. An example is a text file that contains documentation, such as a Readme file.

So when you choose None, they are actually excluded from the project and you can not do any operation such as copy task and just as explanatory documents.

Solution

Please change None to Content so that they will include into the projects and you can build the project successfully without any errors.(It works in my side)

Also, you can refer to this document to know the parameters of the build action.

Edit:

After l followed the build steps of the instructions-----run the bootstrapper.ps1 in powershell, l have got the error like:

Since the first error, l have found in the path

C:\Users\Admin\Downloads\SkiaSharp-master\cake\native-shared.cake

I think the problem for the first error is that the system cannot capture the path to PYTHON_EXE

var PYTHON_EXE = Argument("python", EnvironmentVariable("PYTHON_EXE") ?? "python");

Just as a suggestion, you can define the variable in the System Environment and then input the specific location for python.exe. If it does not work and for the second error, I think you should contact with the author about it.

Hope it could help you.
